Joyfulness
JOY-ful-nes
n. (the state of being full of joy; gladness)
From joy, Old French joie, Latin gaudium. The Authorized Version uses the noun twice, and they are among the most searching verses in Scripture: joyfulness as the thing Israel failed to serve with, and joyfulness as the fruit of being strengthened for patience.

Biblical Definition

In the long catalogue of curses, Moses states the cause of them in a single verse that has nothing to do with outward failure: “Because thou servedst not the LORD thy God with joyfulness, and with gladness of heart, for the abundance of all things” (Deuteronomy 28:47). The service was rendered; what was missing was the joy in rendering it, and that — in a season of abundance — is named as the reason judgment came. Paul prays for the Colossians in terms that sound, until the last word, like a prayer for endurance: “Strengthened with all might, according to his glorious power, unto all patience and longsuffering with joyfulness” (Colossians 1:11). All might and glorious power are asked for, and what they produce is patience, longsuffering, and joy in the middle of both. Divine strength in the New Testament is not usually given so that the load may be lifted, but so that it may be carried gladly.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines joyfulness as gladness; joy; and the state of being full of joy or delight.

expand to see more

JOYFULNESS, n. Gladness; joy; the state of being joyful.

JOYFUL, a. Full of joy; very glad; exulting; as, the heart is joyful.

GLADNESS, n. Joy, or a moderate degree of joy and exhilaration; pleasure of mind.

LONGSUFFERING, a. Bearing injuries or provocation for a long time; patient; not easily provoked.

PATIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring or fretfulness.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 28:47 — "Because thou servedst not the LORD thy God with joyfulness, and with gladness of heart, for the abundance of all things;"

Colossians 1:11 — "Strengthened with all might, according to his glorious power, unto all patience and longsuffering with joyfulness;"

Deuteronomy 28:48 — "Therefore shalt thou serve thine enemies which the LORD shall send against thee, in hunger, and in thirst, and in nakedness, and in want of all things: and he shall put a yoke of iron upon thy neck, until he have destroyed thee."

Nehemiah 8:10 — "Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength."

Modern Corruption

Joy is treated as a temperament some have and others do not, or as an emotion to be manufactured; Scripture commands it, makes its absence a ground of judgment, and supplies it by God's own power.

expand to see more

Deuteronomy 28:47 is one of the most alarming verses in the Bible for respectable religion. The people served. They kept a form. What God names as the reason for the curses that follow is that they did not serve with joyfulness, and with gladness of heart, and that in a time of the abundance of all things. Duty performed without delight is not a lesser obedience God will accept as second best; here it is the charge. That cuts directly against the common assumption that joy is optional decoration on the real business of faithfulness.

Colossians 1:11 keeps this from becoming a counsel of despair or a demand for manufactured cheerfulness. Paul does not tell the Colossians to try harder to be joyful; he prays that they would be strengthened with all might according to God's glorious power, and he names joyfulness as part of what that power produces, alongside patience and longsuffering. Nehemiah gives the same order in a sentence: the joy of the LORD is your strength. Joy is a fruit, sought in prayer and given by God, and it is possible under a load rather than only after it is lifted.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew simchah (H8057), gladness, joy; tuwb lebab, gladness of heart; Greek chara (G5479), joy; makrothumia (G3115), longsuffering.

expand to see more

Hebrew simchah (H8057) — joy, gladness, mirth; the joyfulness of Deuteronomy 28:47.

Hebrew tuwb lebab — goodness of heart; the AV's gladness of heart in the same verse.

Hebrew chedvah (H2304) — joy, gladness; the joy of the LORD is your strength.

Greek chara (G5479) — joy, delight; the last word of Paul's prayer in Colossians 1:11.

Greek makrothumia (G3115) — longsuffering, patient endurance; joy's companion under a load.

Usage

"“Because thou servedst not the LORD thy God with joyfulness” — the charge."

"“Unto all patience and longsuffering with joyfulness” — what power produces."

"“The joy of the LORD is your strength” — not the reward of it."
